source_locator.description: Opening cave direction after the structural star and before the first labelled utterance.

translation.english_text: (Inside the cave, an invisible figure is sculpting a statue, smiling before it.)
notes: The source noun `அரூபம்` is rendered descriptively as `an invisible figure`; no identity is inserted into the stage direction.

translation.english_text: Victory... the reward won by one who heeds not pain!... A fitting harvest for the suffering of so many years! From now on, I shall accomplish all that I have set my mind on... Kesari Varma! Let joy overflow in those eyes clouded by sorrow. Let the clouds of grief flee far from you. Troubles—henceforth, dust to us...... Ha... ha... ha... Victory; victory;
notes: The harvest metaphor, repeated `Victory`, exclamations and extended pauses are retained to preserve the source's theatrical cadence.

source_locator.description: Two source sentences between the first and second labelled utterances describing Kesari Varman's unseen voice and the continuing tools.

translation.english_text: Only Kesari Varman's voice is heard. The chisel and hammer keep at their work.
Gurudeva! Is it true? Can your eyes not see me!......
notes: `Gurudeva` is retained as the character's form of address rather than flattened to a generic `teacher`.

translation.english_text: Yes, Kesari Varma! You have become invisible. The medicine I discovered has begun to work. What could not be attained has been attained. A magnificent triumph for my research. You can see everyone. But no one can see you.
notes: The source's short declarative sequence is retained rather than compressed into smoother explanatory prose.

translation.english_text: Gurudeva!... Thirteen years... I have burned with one thought—to avenge myself upon that sinner! Now that you have shown me the path at last! ......Swami! Will this invisibility not last long?......

english_page_segments.english_text: Gurudeva!... Thirteen years... I have burned with one thought—to avenge myself upon that sinner! Now that you have shown me the path
at last! ......Swami! Will this invisibility not last long?......

notes: The source utterance crosses PDF 7→8 and remains one English unit with page segments mirroring the source break.
`Swami` is retained as a second reverential address because the source shifts from `குருதேவா` to `சுவாமி`.

translation.english_text: It will not—but we can try further. If I find the herbs I seek, you may not merely remain invisible; you may even become imperishable. But Kesari Varma! Use this so that the good may live!
notes: `அழியாமலே` is rendered as `imperishable` rather than expanded into a stronger claim of literal immortality.

translation.english_text: I will use it so the good may live! At the same time, I will expose this destroyer's fox-like tricks. Sinner! Vindictive wretch................... Bhadrakali who poisoned her own husband! Your poison did not kill me, woman. Kesari Varman is alive! He has not died—he will not die, not before exposing your plot! Cheat!.....glib-tongued trickster!
notes: The source's escalating invective, repeated death-denial and mythic insult `பத்திரகாளி` are retained rather than softened.
`Bhadrakali` is transliterated because replacing the culturally specific image with a generic insult would flatten the rhetoric.

translation.english_text: Guruji.
It's the statue, my boy!
notes: The colloquial address embedded in `சிலையப்பா அது!` is kept as `my boy` rather than dropped.

translation.english_text: A statue, yes! Why am I sculpting her? To rehearse the torture; Vasantha Sena! I will thrust a spear into your eyes—set your hair aflame—those kovvai-red lips!... I will drive sharp needles into them..... Your mirror-bright cheeks! Ha ha ha... I will slash them with a dagger... that body that drives onlookers mad... I will hack it into pieces and fling them away! The wondrous work of invisibility has begun, woman!... Enchantress, the chapter of vengeance by your former husband has begun. Walking serpent!... Dance of destruction itself! Treacherous demon... gnawing spider.........
notes: The violent catalogue is translated without euphemism because its accumulation is central to Kesari Varman's theatrical voice.
`கொவ்வை உதடுகள்` is rendered as `kovvai-red lips`, retaining the Tamil fruit-colour image rather than replacing it with a generic `red lips`.
The source's sequence of vocatives—serpent, destruction, demon, spider—is retained in order.

source_locator.description: Source-visible palace transition beginning with Vasantha Sena's laughter.

translation.english_text: The scene opens in the palace with Vasantha Sena's laughter.
Mad girl! Even now, if I choose, I can become the chief queen!......
notes: `பட்டமகிஷி` is rendered as `chief queen`, preserving the courtly rank rather than reducing it to merely `queen`.

translation.english_text: That is my wish too, amma. But while the Maharani and the prince are still alive...
notes: The intimate address `அம்மா` is retained as `amma` because it marks the attendant's deferential conversational register.

translation.english_text: Maharani—the prince... both are living corpses. I need only laugh, and the throne itself is mine. One bewitching glance—and this whole realm lies at my feet! I am the queen of the Maharaja's love, girl! I need only will it—Vasantha Sena, queen! Her son Vasanthan, prince!
notes: The source's boast builds through short escalating claims; the English keeps that cumulative theatrical rhythm.
`உயிர்ப்பிணங்கள்` is retained literally as `living corpses` rather than softened.

source_locator.description: Bare source-visible location label opening the archival scene.

translation.english_text: In one part of the palace.
Yes, yes—no doubt, Vikata! The king's son is the prince! About that, I have no doubt...
notes: The comic repetition of `சந்தேகமில்லே` is preserved because it leads directly into the named song reference.

translation.english_text: Vasantha! Is that the only thing we have no doubt about?... On any day, in anything, there is not even the slightest bit of doubt in us.
notes: The intentionally absurd certainty is retained rather than rewritten into smoother logic.

source_locator.description: Parenthetical Vasanthan-Vikatan song reference immediately after their dialogue.

translation.english_text: (Vasanthan and Vikatan — the ‘No Doubt’ song.)
notes: Only the source-visible song reference is translated. No absent lyric body is supplied.
The occurrence remains linked to `manohara-song-001`, whose authorship is unresolved.

source_locator.description: Bare source-visible location label opening the archival scene.

translation.english_text: In another part of the palace.

(Before the King's portrait) Swami! Will the day never come when the two of us are united again...? In all my life I have done no harm to anyone! I have forgiven even Vasantha Sena, who ruined my life.... I did so because your deep affection for her should not bring you pain!... And even if I had harmed someone, have I not suffered for many years, wasting away apart from you? Is this punishment not enough? Swami! The birthday of our darling Manoharan is approaching too. Shall we not both kiss the crown of our beautiful, blooming treasure and bless him together—can that day of joy never come again, Swami!
notes: The source's repeated `Swami!` and sequence of pleading rhetorical questions are retained.
`உச்சி மோந்து` is rendered as the parental gesture `kiss the crown`, preserving the affectionate action without adding explanation.

source_locator.description: Opening cave-interior direction.

translation.english_text: (Inside the cave.)
Where are you off to in such a hurry, Kesari Varma?
To the play—I have arranged for those very people there.
notes: The source's demonstrative `அதோ` is retained as a deictic `there` rather than replaced with an inferred identity.

translation.english_text: I had forgotten. Is today Manoharan's birthday celebration? Hmm... what name have you given the play?
The Sword of War.
notes: The play title `போர்வாள்` is translated semantically and is not presented as a source English title.

translation.english_text: Shabash... there is no obstacle to staging it, is there?...
notes: `சபாஷ்` is retained as `Shabash` to preserve the spoken register rather than flattening it to a neutral approval.

translation.english_text: None. Because they will not understand the story...
What alias have you given Vasantha Sena in your play?
Deva Sena!
Your name?
Eeswari Varman. I have changed Purushothaman to Uthama Purushan.
notes: The nested-play aliases are transliterated; they remain derivative character names, not replacements for the outer-story identities.

translation.english_text: They will certainly understand the story.
They must understand it. At least then, will Purushothaman not come to his senses?
notes: The rhetorical question is retained because it reveals Kesari Varman's purpose in staging the disguised story.

translation.english_text: Hmm... try and see!
I shall go, Gurudeva!
notes: `குரு தேவா` follows the pilot's established `Gurudeva` register.

translation.english_text: Be careful.

source_locator.description: Opening palace direction introducing the concealed Ugrasena portrait in Vasantha Sena's pendant.

translation.english_text: (Palace. Vasantha Sena is looking at Ugrasena's portrait, hidden inside the pendant on her pearl necklace.)
Amma... whatever else you may forget day after day, you never forget this, do you? What is there in this pendant that draws your eyes like a magnet?
No magnet, girl! A god who lends a hand in danger!
notes: The source pivots from the maid's literal `magnet` to Vasantha Sena's metaphorical protector; the abrupt contrast is retained.

translation.english_text: A god?
Look... (She shows the portrait.)
notes: The label-attached source action remains inside the dialogue-linked unit.

translation.english_text: Amma, the Maharaja is coming!
Still not finished with your adornment? It is already time for the play...
There—finished.
Have you forgotten? Today is Manoharan's birthday.
Would I forget—the boy's birthday? Another memory came to me...
What is it, Vasanthi?
The thirteenth anniversary of our festival of love.
Yes, my dear... I did not even notice the years flying by.

source_locator.description: Purushothaman approaches and touches Vasantha before Vasanthan interrupts.

translation.english_text: [As he comes closer, he touches Vasantha.]

Do not touch fire! This body will burn you! It may sting a little too—about all this I have no doubt... no doubt.... What is this, Amma, a new lesson today? Amma!... Hey... Appa! Look at Amma's beauty, Appa... If only I got a girl like Amma...
notes: The comic return of `சந்தேகமில்லே` from scene 3 is preserved instead of normalized away.
The colloquial Amma/Appa register is retained to keep Vasanthan's teasing voice distinct.

translation.english_text: Chi... keep quiet!
Was Pillaiyar the only one who asked for a girl like his mother Parvati? What is wrong if I ask too, Appa...
notes: `Pillaiyar` and `Parvati` are retained because the joke depends on the culturally specific comparison.

translation.english_text: This will never, ever end!
notes: The emphatic repetition in `தீரவே தீராது` is reflected in English.

translation.english_text: No doubt.
notes: The brief punchline carries forward the recurring `சந்தேகமில்லை` joke.

translation.english_text: Vasanthi, I am going... get ready quickly...

source_locator.description: Opening location direction at Manoharan's mansion; the following decorative stars remain structural.

translation.english_text: (At Manoharan's mansion.)
Deceit has never lived... cruelty has never endured... Listen to this! The celebration is being held for you... you must come to the celebration...
notes: The parallel opening clauses and repeated pauses are retained as part of Sathyaseelar's admonitory cadence.

translation.english_text: A celebration for me. Wholeheartedly? No... for the sake of convention!
notes: The clipped rhetorical question is preserved rather than merged into an explanatory sentence.

translation.english_text: Wrong, Manohara! Purushothaman is not a man without a father's affection for his son.
It is your wish that he should not lose even that affection! But Father is being poisoned, atom by atom.
notes: `அணு அணுவாக` is carried literally as `atom by atom` to preserve the source image of gradual corruption.

translation.english_text: Whatever it may be, others should not speak this way of dissension within the royal family.
A noble thought! But it ought to have dawned on that woman who ruins the land.
notes: The sarcastic opening and Manoharan's harsh `ஊர் கெடுப்பவள்` description are retained.

translation.english_text: Manohara! Your birthday... if you are not there...
The king will not worry... while that Anandavalli is beside him!
notes: `ஆனந்தவல்லி` is retained as the source's pointed name-like taunt rather than silently replaced with Vasantha Sena.

translation.english_text: Hmm... both of you are being flippant!

Teaching calm is indeed the nature of the wise! But crouching subdued like a tortoise is not the nature of warriors! That woman with the bewitching tongue will come; and my mother must come there too—impossible! I cannot bear to see it!
notes: The wise/warrior contrast and tortoise image are kept intact instead of paraphrased into generic impatience.

translation.english_text: Manohara!
Amma!...
My dear... I came listening all along! Even Rajapriyan flared up—why? Minister... Manoharan will certainly come to the play...
notes: Padmavathi's affectionate address and her quiet assertion of authority are kept in the same cadence.

source_locator.description: Closing source action after Padmavathi says Manoharan will attend the play.

translation.english_text: (Manoharan falls silent.)

source_locator.description: Palace play opening; Kesari Varman speaks from behind the curtain, but the following source lines have an empty printed speaker field.

translation.english_text: (A play in the palace. Kesari Varman speaks from behind the curtain.)
notes: The direction establishes the dramatic situation; the following empty-speaker lines remain unlabelled metadata.

source_locator.description: Opening prologue printed with empty speaker fields after the behind-curtain direction.

translation.english_text: What you are about to see is no tale of fancy, but a picture for thought: the history of an empire ruined by a beauty! King Uthama Purushan was a grove of classical Tamil. The breeze that bathed his mind was Kamalavathi, the crowned queen! The Pandiyan killed the queen's father. Bearing heart-shaking news came a court painter, Eeswari Varman! His wife Devasena was a Chitrangi. She came like a breeze. She turned into a storm. The moment that smiling storm entered...
notes: No speaker label is invented even though the preceding direction identifies Kesari Varman behind the curtain.
The grove/breeze/storm image chain and `செந்தமிழ்` register are preserved rather than summarized.

source_locator.description: The play begins after the unlabelled prologue.

translation.english_text: (The play begins.)
Appa!... Appa...!
Do not cry, Kamala, do not cry!
Did Father-in-law say anything in his final hours?...
notes: The exact source label `வர்மா` remains unresolved in character metadata and is not normalized here.

translation.english_text: There is, Prabhu...

source_locator.description: Empty-speaker quoted message and report following Eeswari Varman's labelled `இருக்கிறது ப்ரபூ...`; spans PDF 13→14.

translation.english_text: ‘My grandson Ajayan himself must avenge the Pandiyan. Recovering my Navaratna throne is his responsibility. Make it clear to Kamalavathi that this burden of vengeance does not belong to King Uthama Purushan... My heartfelt blessings to the Maharaja’—that, Maharaja, is the message your father gave you... As soon as he asked me to tell you these final words, the Maharaja's life departed peacefully.

english_page_segments.english_text: ‘My grandson Ajayan himself must avenge the Pandiyan. Recovering my Navaratna throne is his responsibility.

Make it clear to Kamalavathi that this burden of vengeance does not belong to King Uthama Purushan... My heartfelt blessings to the Maharaja’—that, Maharaja, is the message your father gave you... As soon as he asked me to tell you these final words, the Maharaja's life departed peacefully.

notes: The source prints no speaker label on these continuation lines, so the English unit remains unlabelled despite the obvious dramatic continuity.

translation.english_text: Why are you crying, Amma!
No, my dear. Ajaya, that Pandiyan who killed your grandfather...
Give me the knife, Amma.....

source_locator.description: Empty-speaker continuation immediately after Ajayan asks for the knife.

translation.english_text: I'll cut off his head right now and bring it back.
notes: The source context strongly continues Ajayan, but no speaker label is printed and none is invented in metadata.

translation.english_text: Yes, there is no doubt about that, dear.

source_locator.description: Empty-speaker continuation after Kamalavathi's assurance to Ajayan.

translation.english_text: When you grow up, you will certainly do it...!
notes: No speaker label is manufactured for the source-empty field.

source_locator.description: Padmavathi, watching the play, places her hand on Manoharan beside her.

translation.english_text: (Watching the play, Padmavathi places her hand on Manoharan beside her.)
What is it, Amma...?
Nothing, my dear! The play...

source_locator.description: Source cue returning from the audience to the play.

translation.english_text: (In the play.)
Then I take my leave!
Varmare! You must remain in our palace itself as the chief court painter.
notes: The honorific address `வர்மரே` is kept as `Varmare` rather than flattened.

translation.english_text: My good fortune, Prabhu!
If your wife wishes, she may serve me as a maid.
Our good fortune, Mother!
(To herself) I am a maid; she, the Maharani who rules the realm! If tomorrow the times change...!
notes: The source-attached aside remains inside the immutable dialogue-linked unit.

source_locator.description: Vikatan is shown watching the play before an empty-speaker reaction line.

translation.english_text: (Vikatan is watching the play.)

source_locator.description: Reaction line following the Vikatan-watching direction; the printed speaker field is empty.

translation.english_text: Amma! Amma! She's quite something!...
notes: The preceding direction suggests Vikatan, but no speaker metadata is invented for the empty source field.

translation.english_text: Just like this, a court painter came to the palace... eighteen years ago...
His name?
Kesari Varman!

source_locator.description: Devasena dances to entrance Uthama Purushan; he gives her a pearl necklace.

translation.english_text: (In the play, Devasena dances to entrance King Uthama Purushan. The king gives her a pearl necklace as a gift.)

source_locator.description: Short source cue immediately before Varman addresses Devasena.

translation.english_text: (To Devasena.)
I have happy news for you! On behalf of our country's Kala Mandiram, I must tour the whole southern region. It is the Maharaja's order!
notes: `கலாமந்திரம்` is retained as `Kala Mandiram` rather than replaced with a modern institutional name.

translation.english_text: That is happy news for me! Hmm! You rascal!
notes: The source itself code-switches to `ராஸ்கல்`; the English keeps `rascal` plainly.

translation.english_text: No need to be in such a hurry... I am going to take you along too......
Is it true, Athaan?...... Only now are you my precious Athaan!... Ah!... I have passed all this time like a caged parrot... Athaan—here... I will ask the Maharani's permission and come right back.
notes: `Athaan` is retained to preserve Devasena's intimate register; the caged-parrot image is kept intact.

source_locator.description: Devasena falls down as she speaks.

translation.english_text: (As she says this, she falls down.)
Amma!... Amma!...... Wouldn't listen when told!......
Sena!
Has she fainted again?......
Then, before this too?......
What, master... do not speak as though you do not know. Amma!... in another nine months she is going to become a mother.
Ah... Sena is pregnant.
Then whose son is Vasanthan?
notes: The audience interjection is preserved as the source's pointed parallel between play and reality.

translation.english_text: Watch the play!
A play? Or what actually happened?
notes: The wordplay contrasts `நாடகம்` with `நடந்ததா`; the English retains the challenge rather than reducing it to a simple question.

source_locator.description: The next scene of the play states that Uthama Purushan and Devasena sing the love song identified by the printed words `நிலாவிலே ! சல்லாபமே!!`.

translation.english_text: As the next scene of the play, King Uthama Purushan and Devasena sing a love song — ‘In the Moonlight! Amorous Delight!!’
notes: Only the source-visible title/refrain reference is translated; no absent lyric body is supplied.
The unit is linked to `manohara-song-002`, whose authorship remains unresolved.

translation.english_text: Hmm... it seems the city inspection did not finish early today........
Yes... yes... it has indeed grown late... an unexpected amusement on the way......

Your words are amusing too... Perhaps even my staying awake here is an unexpected amusement to you... Swami...... Are these fashionable clothes for a city inspection?... Fine fragrance!... a box of javvadhu!... Oh!... You look as though you have only now returned from the bridal chamber... Who is your new bride, Swami?...
notes: The accumulating sarcastic questions and the source-specific `javvadhu` fragrance reference are retained.

translation.english_text: Curb your tongue when you speak... go, then—
Has your tongue become this foul? That Chandali's company.
notes: `சண்டாளி` is retained as the caste-marked insult `Chandali` rather than softened into a generic insult.

source_locator.description: The king slaps Kamalavathi on the cheek.

translation.english_text: (The king slaps Kamalavathi on the cheek.)

Maharaja! You have spoken arbitrarily, outside all reason and argument, and struck and hurt me without cause. I am not prepared to see you again; my eyes shrink even at the sight of you. Until the heat of your passion for the harlot Devasena subsides and you come of your own accord to see me, I will not come to see you—remember that well. Maharani Kamalavathi may not possess the beauty of your new Rati-devi. But a day will surely come in your life when you understand that this yellow marriage-thread of hers has a unique sanctity. Go then, to your holy service! Go.
notes: The speech's formal argumentative opening, insult, marital-symbol image and final sarcasm are preserved without compression.
`Rati-devi` and the yellow marriage-thread image are retained because generic wording would flatten the source's register and symbolism.

translation.english_text: You need not tell me! I am already going.

source_locator.description: Source cue `தேவசேனா தோழியிடம்.` before the poison instruction.

translation.english_text: Devasena, to her maid.
This dot is the mark... put the poison in this one. Careful......
Maharaja! I cannot remain here any longer... my heart is boiling.
Athaan... hot milk... the headache will fly away......
Sena, they say women of evil karma mix poison into milk even for their own husbands. Have you heard of that?
notes: The unusual source phrase `கர்மக் கள்ளிகள்` is rendered as `women of evil karma` rather than neutralized.

translation.english_text: No, Athaan... but there is nothing like that in this milk.
When you say so, what have I to fear? Sena, come here...... It has been a long time since I gave you milk with my own hand, hasn't it?........
Yes... all that was in the early days of marriage...
Chi... do not say that... drink...
It is like divine nectar, Athaan!......
All right... give it here. I will drink it myself.
Why... I will give it to you... hmm...
No! No! Poison!
notes: The source-visible audience interruption remains linked to its exact labelled dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Ha ha ha... the poison seems to be working... So this is the way of the clever......
notes: The taunting laugh and ironic `புத்திசாலிகள்` are retained.

translation.english_text: You... Rakshasi!... As though committing adultery were not enough, you poison your own husband to death too? Ah.........
notes: `Rakshasi` is retained as the source's mythic insult rather than softened.

translation.english_text: Are the sufferings I endured because of you one or two? You separated me from Rudrasenan, the love of my life! Now what I carry has flowered, set fruit and is ripening... If I kept you alive, would you not cut away something else too? That is why I got ahead of you... Who can stop your fate? Every fool who does not know how to understand his wife's mind meets this same fate, in every age......
notes: The flower/fruit/ripening metaphor is preserved without over-specifying what the source leaves figurative.
The final generalization about husbands is retained as Devasena's theatrical moral rather than softened.

source_locator.description: Varman dies; Vasantha Sena, watching the play, cries out for it to be stopped.

translation.english_text: Varman dies; Vasantha Sena, watching the play, cries out for them to stop it!

source_locator.description: Source cue immediately before the final unlabelled accusation voice.

translation.english_text: (A voice is heard.)

source_locator.description: Final accusation printed without a speaker label; spans PDF 18→19.

translation.english_text: She killed her husband! Rolled him into the forest torrent... Murderess! She is still alive! She is still alive.

english_page_segments.english_text: She killed her husband! Rolled him into the forest torrent...
Murderess! She is still alive! She is still alive.

notes: The repeated final accusation and its empty speaker field are preserved; no identity is assigned in metadata.

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena's inner chamber; she paces angrily and two soldiers enter.

translation.english_text: [Vasantha Sena's inner chamber. Vasantha Sena rises and paces in fury... Two soldiers enter......]
Where... is the theatre troupe?
We chased them on and on. They escaped......
Brave men! Shameless. Chi, run!......
notes: The opening `தைரியசாலிகள்!` is preserved as sarcastic praise.

translation.english_text: Why, Amma... the actors;
notes: The source trails off with a semicolon-like interruption; the English does not complete the thought.

translation.english_text: Yes?...... To give them a reward!.....
They do deserve one, Amma... even if the story exposed us, the acting was good!
Chi... what is this review of yours... go away, girl! Hmm!

source_locator.description: Source `(தனக்குள்)` block after Vasantha Sena dismisses her maid; no speaker label is printed.

translation.english_text: (To herself) The play... was written around me! Kesari Varman alive... Chee-chee, a corpse coming back to life... perhaps... the poison did not work properly......
notes: Context points to Vasantha Sena, but the source prints no speaker label and none is added to metadata.

source_locator.description: The king enters after Vasantha Sena's internal monologue.

translation.english_text: (The king enters.)
Prabhu!

source_locator.description: The king sits with a foolish/awkward smile.

translation.english_text: (The king sits down with a foolish smile.)
No usual smile... you look worn... what is the reason, Swami?......
Nothing...
Then why has that honeyed word ‘Kanne’ not fallen from your lips? Turmoil in your eyes... Kannala! Milk!...
notes: The source's intimate address words `கண்ணே` and `கண்ணாளா` are retained because Vasantha Sena is consciously performing sweetness.

translation.english_text: Milk?...
Why, oh-ho! Has the play come back to mind?...
Nothing like that...
Why speak through sighs? Ask me directly. My husband Kesari Varman... I had told you that, unable to bear seeing our love, he ran away from the town...
Yes! Now???
In the play Devasena poisons and kills her husband! And you too, believing it to be true......

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena takes both cups in her hands before an unlabelled quoted fragment.

translation.english_text: Taking both cups in her hands...

source_locator.description: Quoted fragment after the two-cup action; no speaker label is printed.

translation.english_text: ‘Of these, whichever you wish, you may...’
notes: The source leaves the phrase unfinished and unlabelled; the English does the same.

translation.english_text: No... you give me one...

No, take whichever you prefer. Suspicion is a troublesome disease. A dagger that cuts a life of love apart... it turns even a warrior into a coward... here, take one... (then, thinking)... no, not even that... I will take both myself.
notes: The disease/dagger/warrior-coward rhetorical chain is preserved.
`சாப்பிடுகிறேன்` is rendered neutrally as `take both` because the source refers to the two offered cup portions rather than supplying a clear modern drinking verb.

source_locator.description: Source `ஆச்சரியமாய்` cue after Vasantha Sena says she will take both.

translation.english_text: (In astonishment)......

Forgive me, Maharaja? For thirteen years I have lived as your chaste wife—I ask on the strength of that. Ornaments—life of luxury—royal pleasures—enough... please give me... saffron robes! A begging bowl in my hand! Do not refuse. Give me leave to go......
notes: The renunciation performance is kept as a sequence of abrupt demands rather than smoothed into a single request.

translation.english_text: Go...... you?...... where, my dear......
The world is vast, Prabhu! In its crowds I will become a mere drop—I will spend my life chanting your name.
notes: The drop-in-the-crowd image and devotional performance are retained.

translation.english_text: They have plotted to set fire to my happy life lying at your feet!
A plot? Who?
The Maharani herself!
Who... Padmavathi?......
No... a brazen lie?... O king who rules the realm... do not be sacrificed to syrupy speech!
notes: `பச்சைப் புளுகு` / `பாகு மொழி` becomes `brazen lie` / `syrupy speech` to retain the contrast and rhetorical bite.

translation.english_text: Look, Swami, look...... What I heard is true...... They say the Maharani is even holding secret counsel...... to separate me from you......
It does need looking into! (To the guard) Search and find who spoke here.
notes: The label-attached guard instruction remains inside the dialogue-linked unit.

source_locator.description: Soldiers run toward the direction from which the sound came.

translation.english_text: (The soldiers run toward the direction from which the sound came.)

A smear of civet on a festering wound! Patience—to sear away that evildoer's false disguise......... Enough, Amma, of all this endurance. Give the order. I will make that woman who ruins the land disappear without a trace!
notes: The source's dense alliterative `ப`-sequence cannot be mechanically reproduced in English, but its wound/perfume/false-mask imagery and accelerating force are retained.

translation.english_text: Manohara! Wait......

source_locator.description: A sword from the box there is given to Manoharan.

translation.english_text: (The sword in the box there is handed to Manoharan.)
Amma! (A sweep of the sword) The masquerader Vasantha is finished!
notes: The source action attached to Manoharan's utterance remains inside the linked unit.

translation.english_text: Wait, my son... I ask you to engage in a holier task than that.
What is it, Amma?
Do you know what sword this is?......
Even in the play there was a sword like this... yes, I saw it......

source_locator.description: Bare source-visible location label opening the archival scene.

translation.english_text: In another part of the palace.
The sword that appeared in the play was a false sword! The one I speak of is a sword of war! That sword belonged to Manoharan's grandfather—the Maharani's father—Athiveera Cherar!
notes: The repeated `வாள்` contrast is preserved instead of compressed into explanatory prose.

translation.english_text: Athiveera Cheran...... the name in the play... Athi Dheera Soorar...... Hmm... then?......
notes: The near-parallel between the historical name and its play-within-the-play alias is kept audible in English transliteration.

translation.english_text: Pandiyan Muthuvijayan... defeated Manoharan's grandfather by an unexpected turn and seized the jeweled throne as well... When the grandfather, wounded on the battlefield, was dying, he entrusted to the child Manoharan the duty of avenging Muthu Vijayan, and breathed his last...... Manoharan's broad shoulders must fulfil his grandfather's wish.
notes: `தடந்தோள்கள்` is retained as `broad shoulders`, preserving the heroic bodily image.

translation.english_text: Yes, Manohara! Muthu Vijaya Pandiyan must be defeated. Flowers of victory must be scattered over the dead grandfather's tomb. Our hereditary jeweled throne must be liberated......
notes: The victory-flowers image and liberation language are preserved.

translation.english_text: Give me leave. I will make a rain of victory pour down. I will shatter the ribs of that worthless Muthu Vijayan. I will make him an example to show that those who use deceit to roll up and seize another's country will themselves be rolled up and crushed like this.
notes: The source wordplay `சுருட்டிக் கொள்பவர்கள் / சுருண்டு போவார்கள்` is preserved through `roll up / be rolled up` rather than paraphrased away.

translation.english_text: My son! My heart is cooled, dear one... You must wash away the stain upon our lineage......
notes: The source's `heart cooled` idiom and stain/washing metaphor are retained.

translation.english_text: The stain upon our lineage comes not only from Pandiyan Muthuvijayan—but from the sinner Vasantha Sena too! This sword will spare neither the madman who beat the drum of victory when we were deceived, nor the treacherous woman who came between your life of happiness!
notes: The victory-drum image and the parallel `not only... nor...` threat are preserved as part of Manoharan's martial rhetoric.

translation.english_text: First do what I told you! Manohara! Go and get your father's permission!

source_locator.description: A war proclamation is beaten out in the street.

translation.english_text: (A war proclamation is beaten out in the street.)

War! Terrible war! A war that will decide our country's honour—its future! Warriors, make ready! One from every household, set forth! We shall break the bones of the worthless—we shall raise the flag of victory. Come! Come! To war!... War! War! War! Dum, dum, dum!
notes: Classified as chant/proclamation while preserving the immutable labelled source-record link and drum-beat ending.

translation.english_text: War! War! Mightiest of warriors! March to war! There are two kinds of war. In one war, cattle graze—that is a hay-war! Another war is merely an akka-war! The war I speak of is the fight in which skulls are smashed! Tiger-eyed warriors! Lions! Leopards! Sheep! Roar and charge! Hmm, set out. Why are you standing there? Cut! Strike down! Kill... rip out their guts......
notes: Vasanthan's intentionally absurd war-wordplay and descending animal catalogue are preserved rather than regularized.

source_locator.description: Warrior dolls now appear in the scene.

translation.english_text: [Warrior dolls now appear in the scene.]
Shabash! Vasanthan—you truly are a warrior.
No doubt... no doubt......
notes: Carries forward Vasanthan's recurring `சந்தேகமில்லே` comic refrain.

source_locator.description: Vasanthan draws a sword that has only a hilt; as Vasantha Sena arrives he shoots an arrow. The source direction crosses PDF 23→24.

translation.english_text: (Saying this, he draws his sword. Only the hilt is in his hand...... Vasantha Sena arrives; he shoots an arrow.)

english_page_segments.english_text: (Saying this, he draws his sword. Only the hilt is in his hand......
Vasantha Sena arrives; he shoots an arrow.)

notes: Preserved as one source-continuous stage unit across the physical page break.

translation.english_text: Vasantha, what is this?
He says he's going to the battlefield... for that......
The battlefield?...... Why should you go there, my dear?......
That is a place for warriors to go...
Hmm!... Give me leave, Amma...
You'll ruin your health...... You don't need this swaggering work......

Mother! Is it you who speaks like this? You, descended from the line of that heroic mother who, hearing that her son had been wounded in the chest on the battlefield, vowed in anguish to break the vessel from which he drank her milk—and who rejoiced when she saw that her son had died with a wound on his back? Is it you who speaks so—coward! Coward!... Coward!...
notes: The deliberately overblown heroic-mother rhetoric is retained without silently correcting its paradoxical source wording.

translation.english_text: Ayyo... fate!......... Vikata! I have sent for the physician—let Vasanthan's treatments begin...... The throne is waiting......

Father!...
Give me leave!...
Manohara! Make the enemy know the glory of the warrior clan! Grind the enemy's arrogance into the dust!
notes: The parallel martial imperatives are retained.

translation.english_text: Bring the victory garland!

source_locator.description: Vasanthi brings the garland.

translation.english_text: Vasanthi brings the garland.
I myself shall place it on my darling...
Rajapriya, warriors do not customarily wear the garland of victory before victory is won.

source_locator.description: Vasanthi's face changes.

translation.english_text: (Vasanthi's expression changes......)
I take my leave—
May you conquer! Long live!

source_locator.description: The two leave.

translation.english_text: The two leave......

Vasanthi!...... Are you angry, my dear—
Manoharan is a boy—forgive him!
I have never once been angry with him—he is the treasure of my desire—my beloved son—he may hate me—but to me he is moonlight—a star! Sugarcane juice!
notes: The moonlight/star/sugarcane-juice accumulation is retained rather than rationalized.

translation.english_text: Vasanthi!......

source_locator.description: Outside Padmavathi's inner chamber.

translation.english_text: Outside Padmavathi's inner chamber.
Amma......
My son...

source_locator.description: Padmavathi takes the tray from her companion and applies the tilak to Manoharan.

translation.english_text: She takes the tray from her companion and applies the tilak to Manoharan...
Come back a victorious warrior, Manohara, so that the mother who bore you and the golden land where you were born may rejoice!
notes: `பொன்னாடு` is kept as the image of the golden native land.

translation.english_text: Amma! If I win, the Ratna throne will return! If not, this blood-soaked warrior's sword will return and bear you my news!
notes: The paired throne/sword return image is preserved.

source_locator.description: Departure by chariot.

translation.english_text: [He departs in the chariot.]

source_locator.description: Garden adjoining the palace at night; Vasantha Sena waits in hiding and her companion arrives.

translation.english_text: The garden adjoining the palace. Night...... Vasantha Sena, alone, hides here and there, waiting for someone...... Vasantha Sena's companion arrives.
Where is Bauthayanar?

source_locator.description: The preceding question is spoken in a low, weak voice.

translation.english_text: [In a low voice]......

Softly... there he is...
[Softly]......
notes: The embedded second `மெதுவாக` direction remains inside the immutable dialogue-linked unit because it is stored there in the source record.

source_locator.description: The companion points; Bauthayanan is seen approaching.

translation.english_text: As the companion points him out, Bauthayanan is seen approaching...
All right... you go ;...
notes: The unusual source punctuation is not smoothed into a new sentence structure.

translation.english_text: Bauthayanar... are you leaving tonight itself?......
Yes... why?...
Act with cunning......
I'll make sure he does not return. Put aside your worry.
His head must lie at my feet.
Uh-uh... bringing the head would put us in danger. I'll kill him on the battlefield itself and show you his war-sword.
Yes—we must put the blame on the enemies. Manoharan's death must remain a mystery—
Oh!
A reward of a thousand gold pieces for you!......
Ammani, I shall bring the war-sword; you, the sack of gold......
Bring me news that fills me with joy—gold? I'll heap diamonds upon you.
All right, Amma...
Be careful......

source_locator.description: Muthu Vijayan's palace.

translation.english_text: (Muthu Vijayan's palace.)
My king! Danger... danger... destruction to the ramparts!
The ceremonial full-pot has been shattered.
notes: `பூரண கும்பம்` is retained as the ceremonial full-pot image rather than generalized into merely 'an omen'.

translation.english_text: The enemies are advancing.
Appa! Must so much blood flow for this Ratna throne?
Blood... blood is a swimming pool to me. War is a pastime to me! Not knowing that, this brute comes crashing against Muthu Vijayan!
notes: The blood/swimming-pool and war/pastime boasts are preserved at full theatrical pitch.

translation.english_text: Danger! Danger! The formations have broken apart.
Where is the commander? Where is that lion-hearted man?
He has won a body of fame, O king! He has fallen on the battlefield.
notes: `புகழுடம்பு பெற்றுவிட்டார்` is preserved as the classical image of gaining a 'body of fame'.

translation.english_text: The fish-flag has fallen.
notes: The source's hyphen delimiter is preserved in metadata upstream; translation does not normalize the source record.

translation.english_text: Ah!... I am setting out now... where are my armies...

source_locator.description: Manoharan's forces scale the fort wall under heavy resistance.

translation.english_text: Manoharan's forces climb the fort wall. Fierce resistance—

Come on, little brother!...
Young man who does not know how to hold a sword! Do not imagine you have encircled the fort.
I have heard that you are a warrior... in the swing of your tongue!
notes: The `வாய் வீச்சு / வாள் வீச்சு` setup is preserved for Muthu Vijayan's answer.

source_locator.description: Muthu Vijayan angrily swings his sword as he answers.

translation.english_text: [Muthu Vijayan, in a fit of rage, swinging his sword...]
In the swing of the sword too!...
notes: The tongue/sword swing wordplay is retained as closely as English permits.

source_locator.description: The fierce duel, breach, Muthu Vijayan's death, victorious entry and flag change span PDF 27→28.

translation.english_text: A furious swordfight rages between the two...... At the fort gate the two armies fight savagely; at last Manoharan's forces begin to enter. Muthu Vijayan falls to Manoharan's sword...... At the fort gate Manoharan's forces enter with cries of victory... At the front of the fort the Pandiyan fish-flag is lowered, and Rajapriyan has the tiger-flag raised......

english_page_segments.english_text: A furious swordfight rages between the two...... At the fort gate the two armies fight savagely; at last Manoharan's forces begin to enter. Muthu Vijayan falls to Manoharan's sword......
At the fort gate Manoharan's forces enter with cries of victory... At the front of the fort the Pandiyan fish-flag is lowered, and Rajapriyan has the tiger-flag raised......

notes: Preserved as one continuous battle-result unit across the physical page break.

source_locator.description: Vijaya's inner chamber.

translation.english_text: (Vijaya's inner chamber.)
He has set, Amma!
notes: The source uses the sunset image `அஸ்தமித்து விட்டார்` for death, retained rather than flattened to 'he died'.

translation.english_text: Ah!
The king embraced a warrior's death with a smile of victory.
Be calm...

Calm? My father is a corpse... the flag has fallen... the crown has fallen...
A vow of victory! I will bring it to an end today itself! Tonight!
notes: The flag/crown fall and immediate vow are kept in the source's clipped escalation.

source_locator.description: Night at Manoharan's camp-house.

translation.english_text: (Night. Manoharan's camp-house.)

source_locator.description: Bauthayanan raises a dagger to kill the sleeping Manoharan.

translation.english_text: Bauthayanan raises a dagger to kill the sleeping Manoharan.

source_locator.description: Vijaya enters in soldier's dress with a drawn sword and involuntarily cries out.

translation.english_text: At that moment Vijaya enters in a soldier's dress, unseen by anyone, with a drawn sword, and without realizing it cries out, ‘Oh!’
notes: The source embeds the cry inside the stage narration rather than printing a speaker label, so no dialogue identity is created.

source_locator.description: Manoharan wakes and catches Vijaya's hand.

translation.english_text: Manoharan wakes, catches Vijaya's hand—
Who are you?
I am neither a ghost given another life in the cremation-ground you created, nor a corpse! I am one among the enemies who escaped your sight—a warrior of the Pandiyan land!

english_page_segments.english_text: I am neither a ghost given another life in the cremation-ground you created, nor a corpse! I am one among the enemies who escaped your sight—
a warrior of the Pandiyan land!

notes: The genuine PDF 28→29 utterance remains one English unit.

translation.english_text: A warrior of the Pandiyan land! Hmm... it seems the first lesson under Muthu Vijayan's rule is military training in lurking and pouncing at midnight, you spineless fellow. Is one of those men left who carry a sword in the hand and cowardice in the heart? Run away... save your life...
notes: The hand/sword and heart/cowardice antithesis is preserved.

translation.english_text: Manohara!... We must not let him go...
Let the poor fellow go... I have forgiven him.
Ours is not a tradition that begs forgiveness...
A tradition of attacking from hiding... great warrior!
Those who cut off a sleeping man's head are warriors too—in the schools of the Pandiyan land! Get out, you worthless coward!
Coward... am I a coward! Look here... I shall take my revenge openly, right now....

source_locator.description: Vijaya draws her sword; as Manoharan stops her, her headcloth slips away.

translation.english_text: [She draws her sword. As Manoharan stops her, her headcloth slips away.]
Ah! A woman!
Your enemy's daughter... the woman who came for revenge...
Princess!
A marvellous sight—a sword in hands that wear bangles!
Do not talk!... If you are a warrior, speak after you defeat me!
History has no record of warriors defeating spear-eyed women, Princess!
notes: The `வேல்விழி` spear-eye image is retained.

translation.english_text: No need for mockery... draw your sword.
My sword plays only on the battlefield... it does not bruise fruit!
notes: The source's fruit image is retained rather than domesticated into a generic chivalric phrase.

translation.english_text: If you have courage—if all that talk about the marks of a warrior was not mere tongue-play—swing your sword... let a good judgement be delivered....

A good judgement... will not be delivered by the sword-point. From now on it must be obtained in the court of law! Tender creeper born of the Pandiyan, you are now a prisoner—a prisoner under protection! Rajapriya! Take her away!
notes: The `பைங்கொடி` tender-creeper image is preserved.

translation.english_text: There is our flag at the fort gate! A flag announcing that Princess Vijaya is Manoharan's slave!

Do not speak! I lived as a princess—I will not live as a slave. I roamed like a skylark—I will not be caught in the cruel grip of vultures. I floated in the breeze of freedom—I will not be trapped in the cyclone of slavery. The lap of death is far better than the feet of an enemy.
notes: The skylark/vulture, breeze/cyclone and feet/lap parallel imagery is preserved.

source_locator.description: Vijaya's inner chamber; the source names the song `வாழ்வதே மாது நான்`.

translation.english_text: Vijaya's inner chamber — the song ‘I, a Woman, Live.’
notes: Only the source-visible title/location reference is translated; no absent lyrics are supplied.
The occurrence's lyric authorship remains unresolved in the song evidence layer.

source_locator.description: Vijaya tries to drink poison.

translation.english_text: Vijaya tries to drink poison.
Vijaya! Suicide is cowardice!
Entering the women's inner chamber in the dark is greater cowardice still...
Never mind. I have saved a flowering creeper from the storm of death.
notes: The flower-creeper/death-storm image is retained.

translation.english_text: No one need stop the death of this slave.
Slave? Who is a slave? You are a princess made of beauty itself...

source_locator.description: Rajapriyan enters as the conversation continues.

translation.english_text: (Rajapriyan enters.)
That is exactly why I say one must not enter the inner chamber at midnight!
Rajapriya! Do you know the news?
I came knowing your news, didn't I! Manohara! This is a time to be on guard. Do not be deceived! A little while ago the princess was Yama himself coming to kill you!
notes: `எமன்` is retained as Yama rather than generalized to 'death'.

translation.english_text: I too have a heart. Those who possess a good heart make a mistake only once.
Vijaya! You are one who must live. More than that, you are under my protection... I cannot permit such disastrous acts.
Life is not your slave. It was given by the Lord.
The explanation for that—tomorrow, in the inquiry hall.

source_locator.description: Pandiyan people's inquiry hall.

translation.english_text: (The inquiry hall of the Pandiyan people.)

She tried to commit murder—she attempted suicide. She has committed enormous, unforgivable crimes, Princess! She stands before the people's assembly! The very lifetime of the young princess who tried to separate our prince, my dearest friend, the jewel of the Chola line—this Manoharan—must be brought to an end. Princess! Prepare to suffer the punishment I give you for your whole life. By sunset tomorrow evening—at the Kali temple—no! I do not wish to postpone the punishment even by one day—for the crime of Vijayadevi, tender creeper of the Pandiyan land, attempting to kill the Chola land's athaan, today itself—right now—in this very place—before everyone—you must place a garland upon Manoharan and accept him as your bridegroom!
notes: The mock-sentencing cadence is preserved so the marriage sentence arrives as the source's comic reversal.
`அத்தான்` is retained as `athaan` rather than flattened to a single English kinship term.

source_locator.description: Pandiyan palace.

translation.english_text: (The Pandiyan palace.)
Vijaya.... I thought you alone were the beauty in this palace. I failed to notice that there is a golden creeper to rival you.
notes: The `பொற்கொடி` golden-creeper image is retained.

translation.english_text: Who?
[Pointing to Vijaya's reflection in the mirror] There! This smile is a sadir-dance of diamond dewdrops upon a golden rose!
notes: The mirror action remains inside the immutable dialogue-linked unit as in the source record.
`சதிராட்டம்` is retained as `sadir-dance` to preserve the cultural dance image.

translation.english_text: Leave that aside! I am the enemy's daughter! Will your mother and father accept me?
I wondered the same thing. I am your enemy, after all—would you accept me?
I loved your valour. The soil of my motherland stopped it! I was enchanted by your charm! My father's affection dammed it back. In the end, your honest heart conquered me! What?
notes: The soil/dam/conquest sequence is preserved as a linked metaphorical progression.

translation.english_text: Speak, my dear... speak! I go on savouring the honey-waves of the sea of your nectar-dripping lips... the love-epics your eyes write and heap before me, queen of my heart... speak a little more...
notes: The deliberately lush lip-sea/honey-wave and eye-written-epic imagery is retained rather than reduced to ordinary romantic prose.

source_locator.description: The booklet names the song `சிங்காரப் பைங்கிளியே... பேசு`.

translation.english_text: [The song ‘Lovely Green Parrot... Speak’.]
notes: Only the source-visible title is translated; no absent lyric body is supplied.
Authorship remains in review in the separate song evidence layer because external attributions conflict.

source_locator.description: While they travel by boat singing, Bauthayanan throws a dagger and misses.

translation.english_text: [As they travel by boat singing, Bauthayanan hurls a dagger; it misses its mark.]
What! Vijaya?
Someone threw a dagger at you and is running away... there!
Some conspiracy is afoot... come, let us leave at once!

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena's inner chamber.

translation.english_text: [Vasantha Sena's inner chamber.]

source_locator.description: Bauthayanan enters carrying Manoharan's war-sword.

translation.english_text: [Bauthayanan enters with Manoharan's war-sword.]
Bauthayanan...
I brought it—the war-sword!
Shabash!...
Ammani!... Manoharan returned victorious... and even married Vijaya...
Then...
Listen—they held a swimming game. I made Vijaya a widow and came back with the sword.
Manoharan is dead?...
Certainly!... Ammani! The reward money!
Here!...

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena gives him the sack of gold.

translation.english_text: [She gives him the sack of gold.]

source_locator.description: After handing over the gold, the source prints the next plan without a speaker label; context suggests Vasantha Sena but metadata remains unlabelled.

translation.english_text: Bauthayanar!... one more task... two hunts with a single aim! If you tell Padmavathi this news, her heart will burst and she will die... after that... I alone am the queen!... you are the Prime Minister!...
notes: No speaker is manufactured because the booklet prints no label on this block.

translation.english_text: Prime Minister?... Then I'll do anything you want...

source_locator.description: Padmavathi's inner chamber.

translation.english_text: Padmavathi's inner chamber.
Hmm... weariness from war—delight with a new wife—how will he come quickly, Amma...!
notes: The `களைப்பு / களிப்பு` fatigue/delight pairing is retained.

translation.english_text: My heart is restless with the desire to see Vijaya!...
Amma... some renunciant says he must see you, urgently!

source_locator.description: Bauthayanan enters disguised as a renunciant.

translation.english_text: (Bauthayanan enters in the guise of a renunciant.)
Greetings...
May you live in well-being... Maharani... first make your heart into iron...
What?...
The news I am about to utter is no sugarcane! Hmm... human life is but a straw in the sea, Amma!
notes: The source's `கரும்பு / துரும்பு` sound-play is represented through the literal sugarcane/straw images even though the Tamil rhyme cannot be reproduced exactly.

translation.english_text: What, Sami; you speak without any connection.
A renunciant is one without ties, is he not!... How greatly you must have rejoiced on hearing that your son had won...
notes: The `தொடர்பு / தொடர்பற்ற` connection/ties pun is preserved semantically.

translation.english_text: Yes, Swami!...
Why does the same heart that embraces happiness refuse to face sorrow?
Swami... what has happened... tell me!
Here... this war-sword will tell you...
Your son has gone... to the world of merit!...
notes: `புண்ணியலோகம்` is kept as the religious image 'world of merit'.

translation.english_text: Ah... Manohara!...

source_locator.description: The source prints `வந்துவிட்டேனம்மா` without a speaker label before saying a voice is heard.

translation.english_text: I've come, Amma.
notes: No speaker identity is manufactured despite the immediate dramatic reveal.

source_locator.description: A voice is heard; Padmavathi, leaning on her companion, starts and turns in disbelief.

translation.english_text: [A voice is heard. Leaning on her companion, she starts and turns, unable to believe her eyes.]

source_locator.description: The source prints `மனோகரா!` in quotation marks without a speaker label.

translation.english_text: ‘Manohara!’
notes: Context strongly suggests Padmavathi, but the source prints no label and none is invented.

source_locator.description: She embraces Manoharan and looks at him in astonishment.

translation.english_text: She embraces Manoharan and looks at him in astonishment...
Why are you looking at me like this, Amma... what happened...? Who is this Sami?... (Seeing the war-sword in his hand) Ah... my war-sword... it went missing... how did it come here...?

english_page_segments.english_text: Why are you looking at me like this, Amma... what happened...? Who is this Sami?... (Seeing the war-sword in his hand)
Ah... my war-sword... it went missing... how did it come here...?

notes: The genuine PDF 34→35 dialogue crossing remains one unit; the embedded stage cue stays inside the immutable dialogue-linked record.

translation.english_text: Manohara! This sinner told me you had left me forever...
Thieving rogue!... Not only has he stolen the sword... has he stretched out a tail too? Look at the beard, the beard!
notes: The Tamil `வாள் / வால்` sword/tail sound-play is represented directly.

source_locator.description: When the beard is grabbed, it comes away in the hand.

translation.english_text: [When the beard is grabbed, it comes away in the hand.]
Bauthayanan...
A new chapter in conspiracy—steal the war-sword and bring it to show her... the Maharani will die. A fine plot...
Scorpion's sting!... Whose plan is this, you wretch!... Speak...
notes: The source insult `தேளின் கொடுக்கே` is retained as an image rather than replaced with a generic curse.

translation.english_text: Manohara, poor fellow... let him go...
We must not let him go, Amma... Rajapriya... lock him in prison!
Vasantha Sena is the cause of everything!
Vasantha Sena! She must not be left alive any longer!

source_locator.description: Manoharan goes.

translation.english_text: (He goes.)
Manohara! Stop—where are you running?...
Amma, what more now—after I have fulfilled your vow!...
I'll tell you. First, ‘put the sword into its sheath!... swear that without my permission you will do no kind of harm either to the Maharaja or to Vasantha Sena!... swear upon me...
notes: The source's opening quotation mark is retained in the English phrasing without inventing a closing quotation absent from the source record.

translation.english_text: Amma!
Swear upon your mother!...
I will do nothing to the king, Amma.
No! It must include Vasantha Sena too!
Vasantha Sena... the vulture circling overhead!... the wolf standing with its jaws agape!... the mountain-python that has coiled around us—mercy for her—??? Impossible! Never!...
notes: The source's `???` uncertainty marks are preserved rather than silently repaired.
The vulture/wolf/python accumulation is kept intact.

translation.english_text: As you wish... let the townspeople laugh that you are a son who does not heed his mother's word!... let the country laugh that I am the mother who bore an ungovernable son!...
notes: The paired townspeople/country and son/mother reproach is preserved.

translation.english_text: Ayyo... it is nothing like that, Amma... here, I swear it now.
My son!...

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena's inner chamber.

translation.english_text: (Vasantha Sena's inner chamber.)
Bauthayanan is a useless little wall!... a cowardly fellow!... He will certainly betray me. If I am to escape, he must not remain alive.
notes: The source insult `குட்டிச்சுவரு` is kept close to its concrete wall-image rather than silently replaced with a different insult.

translation.english_text: Poor Bauthayanan!
Hmm. If one wants to take honey, many bees must be killed... all right, arrange what I told you!
notes: The honey/bees metaphor for eliminating intermediaries is preserved without explanatory expansion.

source_locator.description: In the prison, Vasantha Sena's companion secretly speaks to the guard while carrying a pot; the guard then takes it to Bauthayanan.

translation.english_text: [Prison. Vasantha Sena's companion, carrying a pot, speaks secretly with the prison guard; afterwards the guard takes the pot and gives it to Bauthayanan.]
When the giving god gives, he tears open the roof and gives! Long live Vasantha Sena!
notes: The source proverb is retained through its roof-tearing image rather than replaced by an English proverb.
The source's visible `*` after `தெய்வம்` remains a source-text anomaly upstream and is not silently interpreted here.

source_locator.description: As Bauthayanan unties the bundle, a hooded snake comes out, bites him, and he dies.

translation.english_text: As he unties the bundle, a snake rises with its hood spread, comes out and bites him... Bauthayanan dies.

source_locator.description: Vasantha and the King's bedchamber.

translation.english_text: Vasantha and the King's bedchamber.

source_locator.description: The booklet names the song `பொழுது புலர்ந்தது`.

translation.english_text: The song ‘The Day Has Dawned’.
notes: Only the source-visible song title is translated; no absent lyrics are supplied.
The separate song evidence layer verifies the lyricist as Surabi; that external credit does not alter the source translation text.

source_locator.description: The Ratna throne is carried to the audience hall; Vasanthi sees it and Vijaya bows before Padmavathi.

translation.english_text: The Ratna throne is carried to the audience hall. Vasanthi sees it. Vijaya bows before Padmavathi.
notes: Scene 24 remains a zero-labelled-dialogue scene; no dialogue record is invented.

source_locator.description: Inner chamber.

translation.english_text: [Inner chamber.]
Hmm, tomorrow a victory-festival welcome for Manoharan!... and then I, like a widow, in some corner......
(With discomfort)......... Vasanthi! Do not speak like this—you may come to the assembly with every honour......
notes: The parenthetical emotional cue remains within the immutable dialogue-linked unit as stored in the source record.

translation.english_text: May I come?
Hmm... you may.
Hmm... hesitation has been born... poor you! What can you do? The people of the assembly will not permit it. So what if you are emperor—you must still fear ordinary subjects, must you not!
notes: Vasantha Sena's insinuating progression from hesitation to the emperor's fear of ordinary subjects is preserved.

translation.english_text: No... you may come......

I may come!... What does it matter where I come? On that Ratna throne brought from the enemy land, can this wretched woman—who day and night performs penance thinking only of your love—sit beside you like the chief queen? Am I a sinner blessed with such fortune?
notes: The self-abasing `தரித்திரம் பிடித்தவள்` and ironic `கொடுத்து வைத்த பாவி` are retained rather than neutralized.

translation.english_text: Why merely beside me—if I had strength like Paramasiva, I would keep you even upon my head, like the Ganga!
notes: The Paramasiva/Ganga image is retained rather than replaced with a generic declaration of devotion.

translation.english_text: Then tomorrow...... in the durbar!

source_locator.description: Court hall; cries of Long live Manoharan; the king enters with Vasantha Sena.

translation.english_text: Court hall. Cries of ‘Long live Manoharan!’ The king enters with Vasantha Sena.
Royal honours for Vasantha Sena? The king has truly fallen under her spell.
In that spell, he has bartered away the very honour of this warrior land!
notes: The source record's comma delimiter is preserved upstream and is not normalized here.

translation.english_text: A symbol of disgrace—the king with her... and that too in the royal assembly.
Satyaseelar... what is this?
A firefly in the place where a star should be......
notes: The star/firefly contrast is retained literally.

source_locator.description: Manoharan enters amid cheers and cries out on seeing Vasantha Sena on the Ratna throne.

translation.english_text: [Manoharan enters amid cries of welcome. Seeing Vasantha Sena on the Ratna throne, he boils with rage and cries ‘Ah!’]
notes: The embedded cry belongs to the source stage narration and is not assigned an invented dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Manohara! Your mother's command!
Son......... do you remember........... You said you would wear the victory garland only after winning the war—here is the vaagai garland I place on my darling.
notes: `வாகைமாலை` is retained as the traditional vaagai victory garland rather than flattened to a generic wreath.

translation.english_text: Fie! A victory garland!... from your hand... sword—(he draws it)
notes: The source-attached sword-drawing cue remains inside the linked utterance.

translation.english_text: Manohara... do not disobey your mother's word...
Yes... Manohara!

source_locator.description: Enraged, Manoharan slaps Rajapriyan and leaves quickly.

translation.english_text: Enraged, Manoharan slaps Rajapriyan across the cheek and storms out.

source_locator.description: Padmavathi's room.

translation.english_text: Padmavathi's room.
Amma!
Manohara!... what happened?

What you bound my hands expecting to happen—that is what happened. Amma! Had I known beforehand that you would lay down such a terrible command, I would not have killed Muthu Vijayan—given the lives of so many soldiers—and brought that throne for that sinner to sit upon. She on the throne where you ought to sit? Was an invasion fought for that?
notes: The kill/lives/throne accumulation is preserved rather than compressed.

translation.english_text: Isn't this green parrot the gain that came from the invasion? (She points to Vijaya.) Think of this and forget that, Manohara!
notes: Padmavathi's `பைங்கிளி` image for Vijaya is retained as green parrot.

source_locator.description: After the source direction `(விஜயாவிடம்)`, Padmavathi's quoted instruction is printed without a speaker label.

translation.english_text: Vijaya, calm your husband!
notes: The dramatic context identifies the addressee, but the source prints no speaker label; metadata therefore remains null.

source_locator.description: A part of the palace; the physician is giving medicine to Vasanthan.

translation.english_text: A part of the palace. The physician is giving medicine to Vasanthan......
Hmm... you must take it......
Hey—physician! What's the name of this medicine?
Suyabuddhi Chooranam......
notes: The comic medicine-name `சுயபுத்தி சூரணம்` is transliterated rather than replaced with a modern diagnosis; literally it suggests a powder for one's own sense/wits.

translation.english_text: What is it made from—
It is made with grapes, honey, rock candy and sugar.
Then will it be bitter?...
Uh-huh... a little sour; and I've added a couple of chillies too.
notes: The source's colloquial comic phrasing is retained rather than medicalized.

translation.english_text: Physician!... what disease do I have, man—
An incurable disease...

source_locator.description: The exchange continues onto PDF 40.

translation.english_text: [The exchange continues.]
notes: This unit marks the source's physical continuation without inventing a new scene ending or beginning.

translation.english_text: Hmm—that's what I thought! Everyone keeps saying mad, mad—Vikata! Did you hear? I haven't got any madness at all! It's an incurable disease!
notes: The joke depends on Vasanthan taking `incurable disease` as proof that he is not mad; the comic logic is preserved.

source_locator.description: Cave; the elder is absorbed in discovering a medicinal method.

translation.english_text: Cave. The elder is absorbed in discovering a medicinal method...
Before this invisibility medicine runs out, victory is certain......
notes: `அரூப மருந்து` is translated as invisibility medicine in continuity with the source's established effect.

translation.english_text: The invisibility medicine... has dwindled. A little more...
No need...... Here...... today itself I shall discover a sanjeevi that does not die...
notes: `சஞ்சீவி` is retained as sanjeevi, preserving the source's mythic medicinal register rather than replacing it with a modern scientific term.

translation.english_text: (Pointing to Vasantha Sena's statue)... Vasantha Sena... I must tear out her heart, squeeze it, and paint this statue red... her eyes...
notes: The source-attached pointing cue remains inside the linked utterance.

source_locator.description: An explosion; the guru falls amid smoke and is carried out, his life wavering.

translation.english_text: [An explosion...... The Gurunathar falls amid smoke. He is carried outside... his life is wavering...]
Kesari Varma... my last... blessing.... Do not rush... make Manoharan your ally... for your goal!... I... I am dying......
notes: The broken dying cadence is preserved.

translation.english_text: You laboured without rest to tell the world of a wonder! The invisibility medicine. You did not even show me that method... Swami! All those who discovered something new vanished without revealing it to others... You too have walked that path... is there such a curse upon this country itself?...
notes: The lament about inventions dying with their discoverers is kept explicit rather than modernized into a generic science metaphor.

source_locator.description: Spring-festival celebration; songs; Manoharan and Vijaya sing. No song title or full lyric body is printed.

translation.english_text: Spring-festival celebration. Songs... Manoharan and Vijaya sing.
notes: Linked only to the source-visible unnamed performance occurrence `manohara-song-006`; no absent lyrics are supplied.

translation.english_text: May this love never, ever change...
notes: The repeated `மாறவே மாறாதே` emphasis is retained.

translation.english_text: What kind of question is this, Vijaya!
No... if you too, like Uncle... were to fall under the spell of some Vasantha Sena—

Vasantha Sena. Do not even utter her name to me!......... That dog in the place where my mother should be......... Unless I make her writhe like a worm fallen into burning embers—and seat my mother in the royal hall... I am not Manoharan.
notes: The dog/ember-worm imagery and oath-like ending are preserved at full force.

source_locator.description: Vijaya starts and rises.

translation.english_text: Vijaya starts and rises...
What?

source_locator.description: Vasanthan rises from beneath the seat.

translation.english_text: Vasanthan rises from beneath the seat.
You stepped on my foot, Anni!
notes: `அண்ணி` is retained as Anni to preserve the family-address register.

translation.english_text: Hey, were you hiding here?
Hmm... if all the women beat you with water and flowers, water-flowers and flower-water, flower-water and water-flowers, you'd hide too!
notes: The intentionally repetitive water/flower word-loop is preserved as comic nonsense rather than rationalized.

translation.english_text: (Laughing...) Brave man...
notes: The source-attached laugh remains inside the linked utterance.

source_locator.description: Vijaya also laughs.

translation.english_text: Vijaya also laughs......
Laugh... laugh...

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena approaches with the king.

translation.english_text: Vasantha Sena approaches with the king......
Vasantha!... Vasantha!...
I'm here, Amma... what, Amma...

source_locator.description: They come there.

translation.english_text: [They come there.]
Amma!... Anna and Anni are laughing at me!...
notes: Family-address terms are retained.

translation.english_text:
The town laughs at your brother because he took the Pandiyan's daughter in marriage. The whole world laughs at your Anni because she became wife to the man who killed her father...
[Grinding her teeth]......
They laugh, do they...... I shall laugh away everything... come, you!...
notes: The source-attached teeth-grinding cue remains within the immutable linked turn.

translation.english_text: You can't do all that, Amma!... Anna is going to make you writhe like a worm—be careful! He just told Anni that. My Anni!

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena speaks mockingly.

translation.english_text: [Mockingly]
Hmm... a deed that even the mightiest warriors cannot accomplish is going to be accomplished by this whore's son...
notes: The source insult is translated directly rather than softened.

translation.english_text:
Ah! What did you say?
[He draws the dagger.]
Watch me cut off that tongue which spat poison!...
notes: The source-attached dagger cue remains inside the linked record.

translation.english_text: Manohara! Let go.
Impossible. Even if you do not protect your wife's honour, I shall protect my mother's honour to the end.
Listen to what I say...
Impossible...... if you have the strength, protect her...
Manohara!...
Athaan! The promise you gave Athai—
notes: Kinship terms `அத்தான்` and `அத்தை` are retained because a narrower English substitution would flatten the source register.

source_locator.description: Manoharan strikes Vijaya.

translation.english_text: [He strikes Vijaya.]
Amma!...

source_locator.description: Manoharan leaves in confusion.

translation.english_text: [He leaves in confusion.]
Vasanthi!... you have crossed the limit.
Swami...
Fie... do not speak!

source_locator.description: Padmavathi's room.

translation.english_text: [Padmavathi's room.]

Amma... Amma... Amma... I have stopped the leaping spear, the sword that gathers up fury. Is this deceitful woman who mocked me greater than all of them? Yet it is she whom I cannot oppose, and I have run back here. Because of whom, Amma? Because of you—because of your command—because of the oath!
notes: The spear/sword escalation and repeated causal cadence are preserved.

translation.english_text: Manohara! Tell me the matter! What happened?
Self-respect has been levelled to the ground; valour has been put up for price. A symbol of disgrace danced in arrogance! Amma! You must change your command at once.
notes: The three-part rhetorical escalation is retained.

translation.english_text: You have sworn an oath, my dear!
Must a warrior become a coward? Must throbbing shoulders droop? No... let me not keep that disastrous oath......

source_locator.description: Manoharan leaves.

translation.english_text: [Manoharan leaves.]

source_locator.description: Vijaya enters.

translation.english_text: Vijaya enters...
What happened, Vijaya...
That sinner, Vasantha Sena... (she sobs and weeps)
notes: The source-attached sobbing cue remains inside the linked turn.

source_locator.description: The king's room; Vasantha Sena knocks on the door.

translation.english_text: [The king's room. Vasantha Sena knocks on the door.]
Prabhu! Vasanthi has come, Prabhu!

source_locator.description: The king paces without opening his mouth.

translation.english_text: [The king paces without opening his mouth.]
notes: The source scene derivative's bracket form is not silently repaired; only the verified action is translated.

source_locator.description: Padmavathi's room.

translation.english_text: [Padmavathi's room.]
She said that? And the king simply stood there listening? Was Satyaseelar there then, Vijaya?
He was.

It was a mother's command that stopped Manoharan. What stopped Satyaseelar...... Did his voice tremble so that he could not speak against that cruelty? Or did cowardice take up residence in his heart? (To the attendant) Call Satyaseelar... go at once... bring him now!
notes: The voice/heart parallel accusation is retained.

source_locator.description: Vasantha Sena looks at Ugrasenan's picture in the pendant on her pearl necklace.

translation.english_text: [Vasantha Sena looks at Ugrasenan's picture in the pendant on her pearl necklace.]
What is it, Amma... why that now...
Haven't I told you... this is the god who gives a hand in danger.
notes: The ironic `god who helps in danger` image for Ugrasenan's portrait is preserved.

translation.english_text: Its help isn't needed now at all.
Leave that... the news you brought...
Manoharan is in a fury. The queen too, after hearing what happened, is terribly shaken......
Don't pile it up... tell me quickly.
They have sent an attendant to bring Satyaseelar at once.
At this hour?
Yes...
In the darkness?
Yes...
Satyaseelar is coming to Padmavathi's inner chamber... at night...
To inquire about the spring-festival incident,

I know, girl... I know why he has been summoned... I know that... that is what must be turned around...
Darkness! Padmavathi's inner chamber! Satyaseelar there! It must be seen with his own eyes! By whom? By whom, girl? We must arrange for the king to see it... we must find a way... come...
notes: The clipped darkness/chamber/Satyaseelar plotting cadence is retained.

source_locator.description: At the king's room, Vasantha Sena's attendant knocks on the door.

translation.english_text: [At the king's room, Vasantha Sena's attendant knocks on the door.]
Maharaja... Maharaja, danger... open the door, Maharaja... everything will be ruined... danger, Maharaja!
What is this?
Maharaja! Ayyo...
Tell me what happened...
Vasantha Sena Amma... she's put up a noose...
Ah!
She's going to die... only if we hurry can we save her...
Where?
She went this way...... Ayyo...... Amma......

source_locator.description: They run; beneath a tree Vasantha Sena stands as though preparing to hang herself.

translation.english_text: [They run. Beneath a tree Vasantha Sena stands as though preparing to hang herself.]
Lord...... take this servant into your sacred feet. All the loyalty I showed the king has become water poured upon barren grass... he is not at fault... it is my fate—I alone must endure it.
notes: The `water poured on barren grass` image is retained rather than generalized as wasted devotion.

translation.english_text: Che! Che? (He runs in.) Vasanthi!... what have you done... what madness is this?
notes: The source-attached running cue remains inside the linked turn.

translation.english_text: No... this is the reward true love has received, Maharaja... I do not wish to remain alive even for a moment longer. I shall close my eyes before your very eyes. That alone is supreme bliss for me, Prabhu!
Vasanthi... don't...
Leave me, Prabhu!
Vasanthi... don't... come here.

Leave me—Maharaja—one request at the threshold of death. Please fulfil it. Do not let the slur ‘Vasantha killed herself’ fall upon you. You yourself kill me—here (she shows the dagger). Plunge this into my heart that carries your memories. I shall not think of it as a knife-thrust. I shall think of it as the last kiss given by my beloved. Hmm... do not hesitate—why the hesitation, Swami?...
notes: The knife/last-kiss reversal is retained without softening its theatrical register.

translation.english_text: Vasanthi... have you lost your senses?
After losing your love, for whom should I live?
Vasanthi... I said it in anger...

Fine anger... if we had delayed a little, a killing would have happened by now... all who live by deceiving must go to the world of bliss... and you must go to Yama's world... fine justice this is, Amma...
notes: The Inba-lokam/Yama-lokam contrast is retained rather than generalized to heaven/hell.

translation.english_text: Fie... why are you philosophizing, girl... without even the respect to remember that we are speaking to the Maharaja?
My heart is boiling, Amma... the queen too...
What...
Shut your mouth... get out of here...
